chunk_text: Chagas disease is caused by the parasite Trypanosoma cruzi and affects people in different regions of Brazil. In this study, researchers analyzed blood samples from 65 chronic Chagas disease patients born in various parts of Brazil to identify the types of T. cruzi infecting them and to measure the amount of parasite DNA in their blood. About half of the patients had detectable parasite DNA. The most common parasite types found were TcVI and TcII, with some patients infected by both types. A few patients were also infected with less common types, including TcV and a combination of TcIII and TcVI. Older patients, especially those over 70 years old, tended to have higher levels of parasites in their blood. Patients

common types, including TcV and a combination of TcIII and TcVI. Older patients, especially those over 70 years old, tended to have higher levels of parasites in their blood. Patients infected with TcII generally had higher parasite levels but were less likely to have heart disease compared to those infected with TcVI. These findings improve understanding of the diversity and distribution of T. cruzi types in Brazil and show that patient age and parasite type can influence parasite levels in chronic Chagas disease.

Leishmania infantum is a parasite that causes visceral leishmaniasis, a serious disease affecting internal organs such as the liver and spleen. This study shows that L. infantum parasites of the same genetic type can exchange genetic material inside the gut of sand flies, their natural insect vectors. Researchers created two genetically modified versions of L. infantum that each carried different fluorescent markers and drug resistance genes. When sand flies were fed a mixture of these parasites, some offspring inherited both markers and drug resistances, demonstrating genetic exchange between identical strains. These hybrid parasites had three sets of chromosomes (triploid) and remained stable throughout their life cycle, including during infection in mice. Mice infected with the hybrid parasites had much lower

These hybrid parasites had three sets of chromosomes (triploid) and remained stable throughout their life cycle, including during infection in mice. Mice infected with the hybrid parasites had much lower parasite levels in their organs and maintained body weights similar to uninfected mice, indicating less severe disease. The reduced disease severity was linked to lower activity of an enzyme called arginase, which is associated with disease progression. This work confirms that L. infantum can mate within its natural sand fly vector even between genetically identical parasites, producing stable hybrids with slower virulence.

This study explores how Salmonella genomic island 1 (SGI1), a genetic element carrying multiple antibiotic resistance genes, spreads between bacteria. SGI1 cannot transfer on its own but relies on helper plasmids called IncC plasmids to move between bacterial cells. These IncC plasmids produce a protein complex known as the type IV secretion system (T4SS), which forms a channel that allows DNA to pass from one bacterium to another during conjugation. SGI1 carries three genes similar to parts of this channel, and their expression is activated by the helper plasmid. The proteins made by SGI1 can replace or combine with the plasmid’s own channel components, creating a modified channel that enables SGI1 to transfer more efficiently than the helper plasmid itself.

Two of these SGI1 proteins work together and are both needed for SGI1’s optimal transfer. Additionally, one SGI1 protein helps it bypass a natural barrier called entry exclusion, which normally prevents DNA transfer into cells already carrying the helper plasmid. This ability allows SGI1 to spread more easily within bacterial populations that already have IncC plasmids. This study used computer models based on locust brain data to investigate how the insect olfactory system transforms dense, synchronized signals from antennal lobe projection neurons into sparse and specific responses in mushroom body Kenyon cells, which are involved in memory. Before learning, many Kenyon cells responded to odors but with low reliability and less selectivity. The models compared two types of synaptic plasticity at the connections between antennal lobe projection neurons and Kenyon cells: spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP), which depends on the precise timing of nerve impulses, and spike-rate-dependent plasticity (SRDP), which depends on the overall firing rate. Both plasticity types made Kenyon cell responses sparser and more selective, with fewer neurons responding but more reliably. STDP was more effective

(SRDP), which depends on the overall firing rate. Both plasticity types made Kenyon cell responses sparser and more selective, with fewer neurons responding but more reliably. STDP was more effective at maintaining distinct responses to multiple odors and improving discrimination between similar smells. Plasticity fine-tunes synaptic strengths to enable Kenyon cells to detect synchronized input patterns, which is crucial for accurate and stable odor representation. The findings suggest that experience-dependent changes in synaptic strength help stabilize and sharpen odor coding in the mushroom body, supporting learning and memory. The locust olfactory system thus offers a valuable model for understanding how neural circuits combine timing and plasticity to process sensory information efficiently.

Natural killer (NK) cells are immune cells that help control viral infections by killing infected cells and producing signaling proteins called cytokines. This study found that varicella zoster virus (VZV), the virus that causes chickenpox and shingles, can infect human NK cells and strongly impair their ability to kill target cells and produce cytokines. Importantly, this loss of function occurs not only in NK cells infected by VZV but also in NK cells that are exposed to the virus without becoming infected. The impairment requires direct contact between NK cells and VZV-infected cells and is not caused by changes in NK cell surface receptors or by substances released into the surrounding fluid. Despite this, NK cells remain capable of releasing

and VZV-infected cells and is not caused by changes in NK cell surface receptors or by substances released into the surrounding fluid. Despite this, NK cells remain capable of releasing cytotoxic granules when stimulated in a way that bypasses early activation steps, indicating that VZV blocks NK cell responses at an early stage of activation. A related virus, herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1), can also infect and inhibit NK cells, though it affects cytokine production differently. These findings reveal a new strategy used by VZV and HSV-1 to evade the immune system by directly blocking NK cell function, which may help these viruses spread and persist in the body.

This study explores how the variability, or "noise," in the responses of groups of sensory neurons affects their ability to represent information about a stimulus. When the same stimulus is presented repeatedly, neurons respond with some randomness, and this noise can be correlated between pairs of neurons. Using a broad mathematical framework that does not assume specific neuron properties, the researchers examined how different patterns of noise correlations influence coding accuracy. They considered several measures of coding performance, including linear Fisher information, the optimal linear estimator (OLE) information, and mutual information under Gaussian assumptions. A key finding is the "sign rule": when noise correlations between neuron pairs have opposite signs to their signal correlations—reflecting how similarly neurons respond to stimulus

information under Gaussian assumptions. A key finding is the "sign rule": when noise correlations between neuron pairs have opposite signs to their signal correlations—reflecting how similarly neurons respond to stimulus changes—coding accuracy improves compared to independent noise. However, the sign rule is not the only way to enhance coding; many diverse noise correlation patterns, including those observed experimentally, can improve coding even if they violate the sign rule. The best noise correlation patterns always lie on the boundary of the mathematically allowed set of correlations, constrained by the requirement that the noise covariance matrix be positive semidefinite and by fixed individual neuron variances. Importantly, under specific mathematical conditions involving the noise covariance and readout vectors, noise correlations can be arranged

the noise covariance matrix be positive semidefinite and by fixed individual neuron variances. Importantly, under specific mathematical conditions involving the noise covariance and readout vectors, noise correlations can be arranged to achieve coding performance as good as if there were no noise at all, effectively canceling noise effects. This noise cancellation is not rare and can occur in large neural populations. Moreover, there is a large variety of noise correlation patterns that achieve near-optimal coding, suggesting biological systems may have flexibility in organizing noise correlations. These results provide a unified understanding of how noise correlations affect neural coding and explain why experimentally observed noise correlations sometimes do not follow simple rules. The study highlights that optimal coding can arise from many different correlation structures, some differing from classical expectations, and that the set of optimal noise correlations forms a high-dimensional convex set on the boundary of allowed correlations.

Zika virus (ZIKV) is a virus spread by mosquitoes that has been linked to babies being born with microcephaly, a condition where the baby's head is smaller than normal. This study looked at stored blood samples from 18 mothers in Hawaii who gave birth between 2009 and 2012—six had babies with microcephaly and 12 had healthy babies. Researchers tested the mothers' blood for antibodies that show evidence of ZIKV infection. They found that one mother of a baby with microcephaly had antibodies indicating recent infection, and three mothers had antibodies indicating past infection. Most mothers of healthy babies did not have these antibodies. Although the number of cases was small and the results were not statistically definitive, the findings suggest

indicating past infection. Most mothers of healthy babies did not have these antibodies. Although the number of cases was small and the results were not statistically definitive, the findings suggest a possible link between ZIKV infection during pregnancy and microcephaly in Hawaii as early as 2009. This timing overlaps with known ZIKV outbreaks in nearby Pacific islands, so some mothers may have been exposed to the virus while traveling. The study highlights the need for further research to better understand ZIKV’s impact on pregnancies in the United States.

This study investigated which bacterial genes help Pseudomonas aeruginosa survive and grow in chronic wound infections, where bacteria remain localized for months without spreading throughout the body. Researchers collected many bacterial samples from human chronic wounds and found that many bacteria had defects in traits linked to causing damage, such as producing proteases, rhamnolipids, motility, and biofilm formation. Using a mouse model of chronic wounds, they tested bacterial mutants lacking specific genes and found that most traditional virulence factors and biofilm formation genes were not needed for bacteria to survive in wounds. The only virulence function affecting bacterial fitness was the type 3 secretion system. Instead, genes involved in anaerobic growth, metabolism, energy production, and maintaining membrane integrity were critical.

Instead, genes involved in anaerobic growth, metabolism, energy production, and maintaining membrane integrity were critical. Further tests showed that bacteria face stresses in wounds such as low oxygen, oxidative damage, and membrane stress. These stresses could be mimicked by growing bacteria densely in laboratory conditions without a host, suggesting that bacteria in wounds mainly deal with stresses from their own growth environment rather than direct attacks from the host. The findings challenge the idea that targeting biofilm formation or common virulence factors will be effective treatments for chronic wound infections. This study investigated how the DNA of phage Mu, a virus that integrates into the E. coli bacterial chromosome, is organized when it is in its dormant prophage state. The researchers found that the entire Mu genome forms a stable loop structure, called the Mu domain, which brings the two ends of the Mu DNA close together despite being far apart in the linear sequence. This loop depends on a special DNA site near the center of Mu called the SGS site, the Mu L end, and the MuB protein produced by the phage. Host bacterial proteins known as nucleoid-associated proteins (NAPs) also help maintain this domain. The Mu domain was observed at different locations in the bacterial chromosome and

produced by the phage. Host bacterial proteins known as nucleoid-associated proteins (NAPs) also help maintain this domain. The Mu domain was observed at different locations in the bacterial chromosome and was not found for another phage, lambda, indicating it is unique to Mu. Low-level transcription from two phage promoters supports the formation and maintenance of the Mu domain, with one promoter’s activity depending on the domain structure. The Mu domain likely keeps the prophage ready for transposition by maintaining the proper DNA shape and proximity of its ends. Additionally, some genes expressed at low levels within this domain may provide benefits to the host bacterium, helping the prophage remain stable over time. This study investigated how zebrafish regenerate their amputated fins, focusing on the role of a gene called lamb1a. After fin injury, lamb1a is turned on in a specific layer of skin cells, where it helps organize these cells properly. This organization is important for the skin cells to send signals that guide bone-forming cells to grow and arrange correctly, enabling fin regrowth. The activity of lamb1a depends on a growth factor called Fgf20a. Without lamb1a, the skin cells lose their normal structure, signaling is disrupted, and fin regeneration is blocked. Notably, lamb1a is not needed for normal body growth or simple wound healing, showing its specific role in regeneration. These findings reveal that lamb1a connects growth factor signals to the

Notably, lamb1a is not needed for normal body growth or simple wound healing, showing its specific role in regeneration. These findings reveal that lamb1a connects growth factor signals to the formation of a signaling skin layer essential for fin regrowth, enhancing our understanding of tissue regeneration in animals capable of regrowing limbs.

This study focuses on Plasmodium vivax malaria, which can cause repeated infections called relapses due to dormant parasites known as hypnozoites in the liver. These hypnozoites can activate weeks to months after the initial infection, leading to new blood-stage infections. The researchers developed a mathematical model describing how hypnozoites behave within the liver and validated it using data from tropical strains of P. vivax. Their model shows that the number of hypnozoites varies widely among individuals, with most carrying few or none and some having many, which leads to more relapses and a higher chance of spreading malaria. The model also predicts that standard malaria control methods, such as mosquito control and treatment of blood infections, reduce transmission but may

relapses and a higher chance of spreading malaria. The model also predicts that standard malaria control methods, such as mosquito control and treatment of blood infections, reduce transmission but may be less effective against P. vivax because of relapses from hypnozoites. Importantly, adding drugs like primaquine that kill hypnozoites in the liver to treatment plans can greatly reduce relapses and transmission. This is because people with many hypnozoites are more likely to relapse and thus receive treatment that clears both blood and liver infections. These findings highlight the importance of targeting the hidden liver stage of P. vivax to improve malaria control and elimination efforts.

Piezo1 ion channels are proteins in cell membranes that detect mechanical forces by opening in response to tension, allowing ions to flow and create signals. This study used cell-attached patch-clamp electrophysiology to measure the number and behavior of Piezo1 channels in small patches of membrane from cells expressing natural (low) and artificially increased (high) levels of Piezo1. The researchers also used computer simulations to explore how these channels might be arranged on the membrane. Their results showed that at both natural and high channel densities, Piezo1 channels act independently without changing their sensitivity to pressure or their likelihood of opening. This suggests that Piezo1 channels are either spread out randomly or only weakly grouped in small clusters, enabling cells to

changing their sensitivity to pressure or their likelihood of opening. This suggests that Piezo1 channels are either spread out randomly or only weakly grouped in small clusters, enabling cells to sense mechanical forces evenly across their surface. The findings indicate that any strong clustering of Piezo1 channels would require additional cellular mechanisms beyond the channels themselves.

This study investigates the role of a protein called Shugoshin-like protein 2 (Sgol2) in ensuring accurate chromosome separation during the first division of egg cells (meiosis I) in mammals. Sgol2 protects the connections between sister chromatids by recruiting the enzyme PP2A to centromeres, which is essential for maintaining cohesion during this division. Additionally, Sgol2 helps turn off the spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC), a safety mechanism that delays cell division until chromosomes are properly attached, by binding directly to the checkpoint protein Mad2. Sgol2 also recruits the protein MCAK to kinetochores, which helps limit excessive stretching of chromosome pairs. which helps limit excessive stretching of chromosome pairs. Furthermore, Sgol2 promotes the formation of stable microtubule attachments by inhibiting the activity of Aurora B/C kinases at kinetochores. These functions depend on different parts of the Sgol2 protein and specific modifications, showing that Sgol2 acts as a central coordinator. Together, these findings reveal that Sgol2 integrates multiple mechanisms to ensure chromosomes are correctly attached and segregated during meiosis I, highlighting its essential role in preventing chromosome segregation errors in egg cells.

Plants use autophagy, a process that helps protect them from infections by breaking down unwanted components inside their cells. This process involves proteins like ATG8CL and cargo receptors such as Joka2, which help target specific materials for degradation and support the plant's defense against pathogens. The study examined how the potato blight pathogen Phytophthora infestans interferes with this defense system. Researchers found that the pathogen produces a protein called PexRD54 that binds strongly to the plant's ATG8CL protein and increases the formation of autophagosomes—structures that carry materials to be broken down. However, PexRD54 also displaces the plant's cargo receptor Joka2 from ATG8CL, weakening the plant's resistance. Experiments showed that increasing Joka2 levels reduced disease symptoms, but this protective effect was blocked when PexRD54 was present. Overall, the study reveals that PexRD54 hijacks the plant's autophagy machinery to promote infection by outcompeting a defense-related protein, highlighting a sophisticated way pathogens can undermine plant immunity.

This study investigated the roles of two related proteins, TBP and TBP2, in activating muscle genes during muscle cell development and repair. The Pre-Initiation Complex (PIC), which initiates gene activity, includes TBP as a key component. Earlier research suggested that during muscle formation, TBP might be replaced by TBP2 to activate muscle genes. However, this study found that TBP2 is not present in muscle cells or muscle stem cells during differentiation, and mice lacking TBP2 show normal muscle repair after injury. Instead, TBP and other parts of the TFIID complex remain present, though at reduced levels, and are necessary for activating muscle genes. When TBP was experimentally reduced in muscle cells, these cells failed to develop properly into muscle fibers,

remain present, though at reduced levels, and are necessary for activating muscle genes. When TBP was experimentally reduced in muscle cells, these cells failed to develop properly into muscle fibers, showing that TBP is essential for muscle gene activation. Overall, the findings demonstrate that TBP, not TBP2, is the critical protein for muscle gene expression during muscle cell differentiation and regeneration.

This study investigated the protein PALB2, which works with BRCA1 and BRCA2—proteins linked to breast cancer and Fanconi anemia—to help repair damaged DNA. PALB2 acts as a scaffold connecting these proteins and also binds directly to DNA, although the role of this DNA binding was not well understood before. The researchers identified a key DNA-binding region in PALB2 and showed that mutations in just four amino acids within this region reduce the cell’s ability to repair DNA damage by about half. They also found that this part of PALB2 can promote important DNA repair activities on its own, even without other proteins usually involved in the process. Additionally, PALB2 can work with RNA as well as DNA, suggesting it might

promote important DNA repair activities on its own, even without other proteins usually involved in the process. Additionally, PALB2 can work with RNA as well as DNA, suggesting it might have broader roles in DNA repair linked to gene activity. These findings highlight that PALB2’s ability to bind DNA is essential for effective repair of damaged chromosomes, which helps protect cells from becoming cancerous. Understanding how PALB2 functions could improve knowledge of cancer development and guide future research on DNA repair mechanisms.

This study explored how the electrical charge on protein surfaces affects their movement inside the cytoplasm of three microorganisms: Escherichia coli, Lactococcus lactis, and Haloferax volcanii. Using green fluorescent proteins (GFPs) engineered to have different net charges, the researchers found that in E. coli, proteins with positive charges moved much more slowly—up to 100 times slower—than negatively charged or neutral proteins. This slowdown is mainly caused by positively charged proteins binding to ribosomes, the cell's protein-making machines. In Lactococcus lactis and Haloferax volcanii, the effect of positive charge on slowing diffusion was less pronounced, likely because their higher internal salt concentrations reduce these electrostatic interactions. Additionally, how positive charges are spread over the protein surface influences diffusion speed, with uneven

diffusion was less pronounced, likely because their higher internal salt concentrations reduce these electrostatic interactions. Additionally, how positive charges are spread over the protein surface influences diffusion speed, with uneven charge distribution causing slower movement. When cells experienced increased crowding, protein diffusion slowed further. Analysis of the natural proteins in these organisms showed that most cytoplasmic proteins carry negative charges, which may help them avoid slow movement caused by binding to ribosomes. These findings suggest that ribosome surface properties influence which proteins can move efficiently inside cells, affecting overall protein mobility and cellular function.

This study investigated how nerve cells recycle synaptic vesicles (SVs), which are small sacs that store and release chemical messengers for brain communication. When nerve cells are strongly stimulated, SVs release their contents and their membranes are rapidly taken back into the cell through a process called bulk endocytosis, forming large structures known as bulk endosomes. These bulk endosomes then serve as sources for generating new SVs. The researchers studied nerve cells from mice lacking two proteins, dynamin 1 and dynamin 3, which are important for a common recycling method called clathrin-mediated endocytosis (CME). They found that bulk endocytosis still occurred normally or was even increased without these proteins, and new SVs were still formed from bulk endosomes, although this

called clathrin-mediated endocytosis (CME). They found that bulk endocytosis still occurred normally or was even increased without these proteins, and new SVs were still formed from bulk endosomes, although this reformation was slower. Detailed microscopy showed that clathrin-coated pits appeared only on the cell surface and not on bulk endosomes, and removing clathrin did not further reduce SV recovery. These findings reveal that during intense nerve activity, nerve cells use a recycling pathway that does not require dynamin 1, dynamin 3, or clathrin to regenerate SVs from bulk endosomes. This improves our understanding of how nerve cells maintain communication under high demand and highlights alternative mechanisms for vesicle recycling beyond the well-known clathrin-dependent pathway.

Macropinocytosis is a process used by cells, including amoebae like Dictyostelium, to take in large amounts of fluid from their environment, which helps them gather nutrients and other molecules. This process involves the cell membrane forming cup-shaped structures called macropinocytic cups, whose walls are pushed outward by actin protein filaments. Researchers found that these cups form around patches of signaling molecules such as PIP3, active Ras, and active Rac. Around these patches, a ring of active SCAR/WAVE protein is recruited to the edges, which promotes actin polymerization and helps build the cup walls. The formation of these signaling patches does not depend on the surrounding actin ring, and increasing Ras activity leads to larger patches and cups. Most new macropinocytic

the cup walls. The formation of these signaling patches does not depend on the surrounding actin ring, and increasing Ras activity leads to larger patches and cups. Most new macropinocytic cups form by splitting from existing ones rather than by folding of membrane ruffles. Similar patterns of signaling and SCAR rings are also seen in related structures like phagocytic cups and basal actin waves. These findings suggest that macropinocytic cups arise through a self-organizing process where patches of active Ras, PIP3, and Rac recruit SCAR to their edges, driving actin ring formation and cup extension. During early development, cells divide rapidly without growing, causing them to become smaller with each division. The mitotic spindle, a structure made of microtubules, separates chromosomes during cell division and must adjust its size to fit the shrinking cells. This study used extracts from frog (Xenopus laevis) embryos at different developmental stages to recreate spindle formation in the lab. They found that spindle size decreases as cells get smaller, mainly because of increased activity of a protein called kif2a that destabilizes microtubules. In early large cells, kif2a is kept inactive by another protein, importin α, which binds to kif2a and prevents it from shrinking the spindle. As development proceeds and cells become smaller, importin α moves to the cell membrane,

by another protein, importin α, which binds to kif2a and prevents it from shrinking the spindle. As development proceeds and cells become smaller, importin α moves to the cell membrane, reducing its availability in the cytoplasm and allowing kif2a to become active and reduce spindle size. Changing spindle size in embryos affected how the spindle oriented itself during metaphase but did not disrupt chromosome separation. This work shows that spindle size is controlled by a balance between kif2a and importin α, linked to cell size through the redistribution of importin α between the cytoplasm and membrane. Understanding this mechanism helps explain how cells coordinate internal structures with changing cell size during development.
